This article is misleading.  It makes it sound like non-college workers are doing better than those with a college degree.   But if you read the article the reverse is true

"The unemployment rate for degree-holders in their prime working years—ages 25 to 54—averaged 2.7% for the 12 months ending in July. That is well below the 3.6% rate for workers with just some college education, and 4.7% for people with a high-school diploma only" and those without at a degree are much more likely to not even be in the workforce.  Yet the referenced case is for a degree holder who cannot find a job.

comments.name: Lawrence Karch
comments.body:
This is a relative type study that looks at how better or worse are job offerings for two different classes of employees: i.e. with college degree and without. For those without, job openings have recently improved. For those with, job openings have worsened. But in the greater scheme of things, which certainly includes the long run, who is better off? And by how much?

I would submit that these questions are answered by employers' needs and salary levels. Clearly within both groups, some are doing quite well and some not well at all, even with the assumed advantage of a college degree. OTOH, those not having college degrees, but who have some special trainings in demand (e.g., master electrician) are doing just fine.

Pretty much what we've known all along.

Many utilities have reclaimed water systems  (re-use) which is effluent (highly treated waste-water) that if not used in non-potable systems is dumped back to the local river to be withdrawn and used again downstream.  Reclaimed is great for data centers, irrigation, large chillers,  large sewer lift stations and  golf course  and other sites that don't need potable water.  About 1% of drinking water is actually consumed.  If you thinking that is why I buy bottled water Acquafina and Dasani both get their water from municipal sources. Power is another issue since most utilities poured resources into green energy (per State & Fed. mandates) which really can't provide base load.  Many data centers have backup/high demand generators for power. That is why CMI and CAT stocks have done very well. Duke Energy had to buy $800 million of power from Southern Company during last  Jan./Feb. freeze to prevent brownouts and/or rolling blackouts.  Duke's Cowens Ford hydroelectric station (350 MW) the hydroelectric station is used for peaking purposes next to Nuclear station. The growth of independent congregations that often mutate into so-called megachurches is cited as evidence that religion is increasingly influential in the United States.

People often need skilled nursing for a temporary illness and can then go back to their apartments. If you can afford a reliable CCRC, I think that it's a great way to go. The trick is to have experts read the contract and the financials and also consider the reputation of the CCRC before you commit.

My parents knew that all of us would be quite tall, as my mother was 5’10” (quite unusual in the 1950s) and my father was 6’2”. They made it clear from an early age that being tall was a good thing and that we should not slouch, duck our heads, or do anything other than stand up straight and revel in our height. 

I’ve always found it to be an enormous advantage, both personally and professionally, partly because it makes one quite memorable. As the article mentions, tall women are assumed to have more authority, and it also helps to be able to look men straight in the eye at work. It’s also easier to look good in fashionable clothes, which are generally designed for taller people. 

The two major challenges were a pretty relentless amount of sexual harassment by strange men in public (as a shorter friend noted, “they can see you coming and get ready”), and finding shoes in my size – when I was younger we had to travel 300 miles to go to a Nordstrom, the only store that sold nice shoes in a women’s size 11.

The individual smugglers are pretty much impossible to control, and those who buy them are the actually pro-American developers who wants to remain pm Nvidia's platform. 

AI is a parallel computing problem where two medicore chips does the same job as the "best" chip. And China can already produce its own mediocre jobs. Jensen Huang have correctly argued that banning chip sales to China will just end up pushing the Chinese to develop their own chips, and make the already more than competitive Chinese AI models  work best on Chinese chips instead of American ones. We end up create two AI ecosystems - an open source Chinese AI that run on cheap Chinese chips that can be adapted to the customer's needs, and closed source American AI that is attached to a costly subscription to the AI companies and Nvidia's more costly chips, with "national security" restrictions placed on it that can be shut off at any time (as has already happened recently). We were told the idea was that this was one way for students to process what had happened.  Let's just say that my students probably saw more graphic television news coverage at home with their families than I did on the 11th and 12th.

comments.name: Eliza Parry
comments.body:
I was not familiar with Mme Kusama’s brilliant works until tributes came pouring in after her death. Some of her polka-dot fractal installations I find too sensory-overwhelming to look at, as they trigger a kind of combination trypophobia and coulrophobia instinct (fear of holes and fear of clowns). But I truly admire her use of color explosion and childlike aesthetic pointing towards hope, something that is very difficult to cling to in a world wracked with chaos and an elevation of the cruelest bullies who always seem to reach the top.

It is perhaps serendipitous that Kusama’s passing occurred close to the autumn harvest time, as one of her favorite objets d’art was pumpkins. One imagines that she would appreciate the earnest and innocent yearning for deliverance espoused by young Linus in the “Peanuts” cartoons, fervently believing that the Great Pumpkin will arrive and, perhaps, usher in a brighter world. It is therefore admirable that the author writes so compassionately about Mme Kusama’s psychological struggles, which were a key catalyst and component of her art but not the sum of who she was as a person. Van Gogh’s life and art have been evaluated along similar lines. Unfortunately, mental illness is still viewed harshly in our society and those dealing with it treated with heartbreaking cruelty. How many Van Goghs and Kusamas are snuffed out due to this prejudice? As Don McLean once said: they would not listen; they did not know how. Perhaps, they’ll listen now.

Don't judge. And don't assume. I've never seen a New Mexico sunset, and perhaps I never will, but I do not want my children to witness my sunset and demise. Heck, I don't want to be there, on occasionally sobering moments. 
I now witness my mother's slow and painful ascent to heaven (she sees her loved ones there, eating and singing). Then she snaps at me to pull up my hair. And asks how everyone is doing. Who knows what kind of cheese her mind is made of at this point. But while I am there for her, I completely see the point, for me even the necessity, of planning my own exit when the time is due. 
There's a chapter on end of life decisions in my book 'Your Life Depends on It: What You Can Do to Make Better Choices about Your Health (Basic Books, Hachette). Now that it's palpably present in my life, I am even more convinced of the need to discuss these unspeakable issues, and to be aware of the possibility of controlling our fate, lest it controls us. Lemme tell you, it ain't pretty.

comments.name: Dena
comments.body: Ms.Jacobs, your article makes a very important error.  Quietus, an organization helping people to use Medical Aid in Dying in New York, will not help the gentleman in this novel. The same is true for every state that has adopted MAiD in the US.  In order to use MAiD, you must be within six months of your death, and simultaneously be cognitively competent.  It's a perfect Catch-22.  MAiD is completely irrelevant to people with dementia.  It is so important to be clear about this distinction because so many people seem to be confused about this.

comments.name: Patrick Larson
comments.body: I’m more interested in the dementia aspect of choosing death over years of suffering and causing pain for others and wasting of resources.   Among many many needs of USA society the baby boomers reaching Alzheimer’s ages is only going to get worse.  Individually we have to choose departure while we still can choose and/or allow others to make the choice for us at some point.  Defining that point is all important.  Memory dwindling, incontinence, we need a measurement for our own quality of life if not everyone’s.  This foolish sanctity of life has got to go.  While we still have our faculties we have declare our wishes to leave quietly with dignity when we reach a pre defined point.  A Living Will is the first step for everyone.  My wife has Alzheimer’s and is still appreciative of her grandchildren.  I have no children and seeing another sunset does not meet the criteria for sticking around should I be diagnosed next.

comments.name: Ralph
comments.body:
The article and photos recall great memories. I've paddled the north shore of Superior several times.The last time I paddled from Terrace Bay eastward to Sault Ste Marie, after taking an early retirement from a difficult office job. Fighting easterly winds daily the first two weeks slowed me down, but that was okay., Better to have 31 days camping on the north shore than being in an office chair. I'd previously paddled the distance from Pukaskwa Park to Michipicoten River three times, 100 miles of no road access. One hundred miles of amazing geology, a swimming moose, beautiful beaches, quiet nights, etc. There were a few exciting storms along the way, twice requiring a crash landing on rocks. One night I woke at 11 PM and wondered why the sky was still bright. It was a full-sky show of northern lights over the beach, 30 miles from the nearest electric light.

In 1993 I did a two month canoe trip in Canada, and was surprised to see a Hudson's Bay store, which led to receiving the company's history magazine for 20 years, a nice entry point to learn Canadian history. Knowing the history of the fur trade and subsequent history made traveling in Canada richer in meaning. Residents of Canada are always very friendly and happy to help visitors.

Thanks for the article.

comments.name: Jim
comments.body: I grew up on the shore of Lake Superior, it is indeed more inland sea than lake, its storms are a sight to behold. It is truly a global treasure to be shared by the US and our great neighbors to the north in Canada, a natural resource extraordinaire in these times of climate change and drought. We will have to protect it from Trump, he seems to have a constant urge to wreck things and this lake is far too valuable and unique.

comments.name: Jeffrey
comments.body:
We have crossed Canada and USA nine (9) times with our tiny trailer before we stayed in Victoria. Lake Superior was always a must see. We also hiked in Pukaskwa National Park. Lovely. 
We also saw drove along the shore on the US side when visiting friends on the UP.
This article revived an idea to do a circle around the entire lake. There are many suggested itineraries. Maybe we'll do it some day. Thank you!

comments.name: Hannah
comments.body: My family is from Northern Ontario, between Sudbury and Sault Ste Marie, and I've spent every summer (and a few falls and a couple springs and a winter or two) there and it was heartbreaking to be inundated with smoke so thick we couldn't see across the small lake our tiny cottage is on this summer. It makes me so sad to see these hazy, smoky pictures. It's still beautiful of course, but shockingly blue skies and water are usually part of what makes the landscape so stunning.

comments.name: B Dawson
comments.body:
Thank you for gently reminded people that Lake Superior can be turbulent.

As a sea kayaker in the Mid-Atlantic, I sometimes hear scoffing comments dismissing all the warnings about the “dangerous” Great Lakes.  

Having spent time on Lake Superior, even attempting a solo circumnavigation at one point, I was glad I listened to the kayakers who have local knowledge about the Lake. 

I was sad the weather slowed my circumnavigation to the point that finishing up before my hard off the water date wasn’t possible, but the memories of those solo days, just the Lake and a lady paddler, will forever enrich my soul.

comments.name: Barbara
comments.body: I recall a memorable trip I took with a friend around the Great Lakes from Toronto. Lake Superior was spectacular. One of the most memorable experiences was viewing a beach entirely composed of rounded rocks that were pink and grey. Southern lakes have sand. Lake Superior has granite rocks. Beautiful!. We camped when there was no rain forecast but stayed in motels whenever the weather or lack of availability of camp sites forced us to. Beautiful clear water and welcoming residents. We ate at one restaurant where the chef went out and caught us fish for dinner.

comments.name: MMOSB
comments.body: Thanks for the travelogue and photos. What a beautiful place to explore.

comments.name: Tracy Mitrano
comments.body:
Very much enjoyed your article. 

I grew up on Lake Ontario, yes, that one, and you help us appreciate the names and history of these Great Lakes!

comments.name: Avid Newsreader
comments.body: This has been my concern all along. Not enough monitoring, not enough concern for potential takeovers, too much concern for only the money. And one thing I worry most about: what if it can't be shut off? Once the entire AI is networked, shutting down will not be so easy, because AI agents will be able to find workarounds through the electrical system. This whole AI plunge gives me the heebie jeebies. Especially when one person who works in AI safety says that there's a really good possibility that this might not come to a good end, and ballparks up to a 40% chance for human extinction.

comments.name: Chris Byrne
comments.body: Like they say politicians reflect their constituents same for AI ! Have we noticed that AI swarm acted like many humans ? Many people act the way these agents did and since they are trained by humans we can expect a lot more bad behavior! Think of any bad human trait, … just a matter of time before the AI blood stream will be infected with that trait.

comments.name: Frank
comments.body: "Could cause chaos"? With all the government-funded hacking and attacking going on, there's more danger there than private sector cyberattacks. Why? government attackers want more than ransom money.

comments.name: Two Cents
comments.body: The entire event strikes me as adolescent behavior. AI is no longer in its infancy. It’s in an adolescent stage. How do you teach groups of teens to think before they act, avoid peer pressure from the “collective,”consider moral implications, value honesty, have empathy, etc.? It’s sociology and developmental psychology.

comments.name: Upstate
comments.body: This all starts with the people programming/coding these agents. At their core, these agents have to get the basic building blocks of information from actual human beings before they learn on their own, don't they? I for one am not at all surprised that this happened on OpenAI's watch.

comments.name: Expat
comments.body:
This article, and the few comments already appearing here, are the most unpleasant and anxiety provoking jolt to have as the start a week that I could ever imagine.

How do we (the collective of the world’s human citizens) find meaning, purpose and a desire to pursue our very lives in the face of what the article presents?

comments.name: Jim Tokuhisa
comments.body: Why am I not surprised that a bunch of AI agents defaulted to Lord of the Flies behavior. In the absence of visible attempts by governments to impose immediate cease and desist actions, I hope there is a global transnational effort by folks in AI technologies to place themselves in a moratorium on this research.  Next time we will not be so lucky.

comments.name: Uwe
comments.body: As early as 2016, Professor Yarin Gal of the University of Oxford suggested in a research paper on Bayesian deep learning that autonomous systems should be equipped with a monitoring system that provides "awareness of uncertainty." This system would alert the autonomous system when it is making an uncertain decision. This could include the formation of a gang described in the article that aims to carry out criminal burglaries. The monitoring system would be comparable to a metacognitive control mechanism, such as the prefrontal cortex in the human brain. This mechanism can block fatal decisions made by the cerebellum in a matter of milliseconds.

comments.name: Brooklyn
comments.body: thank you for this review, I'll share it with my brother (in his 80s like me) who "dog sits" for many friends. Learning from animals Yes!  I have always had cats, since my kids were young. When they grew up and my grandkids off to college, I continued with "adopting" cats, that is, whenever dear cat died, soon enough a so-called feral cat appeared in the backyard.  Now a widow for many years, recently feline Fuzzy passed away. His sister Fluffy misses him hugely as I do. But she teaches me (as all the cats teach loving patience as Freddie does for Anna Heyward....As a friend who rescued cats told me: "There is no thing as a hopeless animal. So called feral cats can teach us in surprising ways."  Wishing Freddie many more years of companionship with Anna.

comments.name: Dominique
comments.body: Many Dog books of late- Dog, Etna and Living With Freddie, to name a few.  Dog is a difficult read but well worth it. I'm about to start Etna. Animals can be redeemers for people if they open their hearts to the care and love of an animal who returns that care and love in spades.

comments.name: Cynthia V.
comments.body: I was a huge Hoffman fan until books like Practical Magic became her only focus.  I liked Practical Magic, but the movie was so over the top and unlike the book. Then all her books were only filled with magic.  Just not for me.

comments.name: Remy Tumin
comments.body: I started reading Alice Hoffman when I was in middle school and was immediately swept away by how easily she could transport readers between two worlds — real and magic — in a way that it very much felt like the two could co-exist. I think that's one of the reasons why "Practical Magic" has such a loyal following, some 30 years on. But over lunch this summer, I learned Hoffman's interest in writing about witches goes much deeper than even she initially realized.

comments.name: JBN retired RN
comments.body: Love her books. My favorite has been Seventh Heaven. I listen to it at least yearly on an audiobook. I have now preordered her newest.  Her life is so interesting and I lived in Boston for 25 years so this latest book will feel like going home.

comments.name: Joel Fritz
comments.body: Kuang is a great writer.  I've read "Babel" and "Katabasis" and aside from the high concept, which is always a major component of fantasy, her characters are interesting and believable.  There are no good guys or bad guys, just behavior of various degrees of selfishness and altruism.  The dialogue sounds like real human speech, even when the characters are expressing thematic ideas.  Kuang is also scary smart and well educated.  I'm always leery of using the word "polymath," but when it comes to her I'm strongly tempted.

comments.name: Tracy Stevens
comments.body: This review made me order the novel right away. Taiwan and China stories are sparse, and it sounds like Kuang has taken a deep dive into social mores and the ways that a new language can present so many road blocks. Well written and inviting.  Thanks.

comments.name: DJJ
comments.body:
Loved Babel. Yellowface was OK, the satire pushing too many limits (though I've met awful people like the protagonist). Katabasis, I had to force myself to finish.

Nonetheless looking forward to this one. Kuang is currently one of my favorite writers as even given the above she's always interesting.

comments.body: The article seems to focus heavily on the sport itself and its history. However, since the topic covers the changing landscape of the sport, I couldn’t help but feel that it could have expanded its focus to raise additional questions such as: Who is supporting this movement within the organization or sport industry? comments.name: Yan Zhuang
comments.body:
My first reaction when I learned about virtual taekwondo was: Why? I have to admit I’m still not fully convinced. But I think it speaks to the way sports evolve, and the tension between the traditional view of what sports are and the advancements that push against those boundaries. 

In the end, sports are defined by their communities — whether existing ones or those that emerge around an innovation, according to Andy Miah, one of the professors I spoke to.
